newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslem refugees protest at U.S., Russian barricade.
newsitem.headline: Moslem refugees protest at U.S., Russian barricade.

text.p: Bosnian Moslem refugees, barred by U.S. and Russian troops from returning home, shouted insults and spat on an American officer in angry protests on Wednesday, witnesses said.
At least two Moslem men were killed and several others wounded as returning Moslem refugees were driven from Gajevi on Tuesday in an exchange of gunfire with Serbs.
At least two Serbs were also wounded in the fighting.
Peacekeeping soldiers from the two former Cold War foes blocked hundreds of Moslems from returning to their abandoned homes in northeast Bosnia.
"Russian bastards, go back to your own country and sort out your own mess," shouted an elderly man, eyes and veins bulging.
The crowd gathered in front of razor-sharp wire barriers and a red and white striped pole that blocked a road between the Moslem-controlled town of Celic and the Serb-controlled village of Gajevi.
Some boys climbed trees on a nearby hill to get a better view of the noisy confrontation and hurl their own insults.

Normally a checkpoint established by NATO-led IFOR peace forces to control military movements to and through a former front-line area, the post is now regulating the flow of civilians into the dangerously tense zone around Gajevi.

"There haven't been any stones today (Wednesday) but someone did spit on me twice. This situation requires some civilian leadership on both the Moslem and the Serb sides," said U.S. Major John Kershaw, a liaison officer with Russian troops at the roadblock.

International Police Task Force spokesman Alex Ivanko told reporters in Sarajevo that the villagers had threatened to bypass the checkpoint and move into the villages -- an option he described as "unwise".

"We've been told there could be as many as a thousand people gathering here today... if they make a break for Gajevi through the woods it leaves us with bad options. We certainly can't shoot them," Kershaw said.

Gajevi was a desolate, litter-strewn shadow of its former self on Wednesday. Most of the village's houses were dynamited flat during the 43-month Bosnian war. The few which still had walls were roofless shells overgrown with weeds and vines.
Blankets, plastic sheeting, clothes, empty plastic water bottles and rotting loaves of bread were all that remained of the small refugee camp which formed up in Gajevi on Monday.

All the Moslems who forged across the de facto ethnic border between Moslems and Serbs in this part of the north- eastern pocket of Bosnia known as the Sapna thumb were forced to retreat after fighting broke out with Serbs around Gajevi.
Serb police said it was the Moslems who provoked a fight and then fled when they got one.
"The Moslems came without any sort of approval and then they started firing at Serbs," said one Serb policeman who refused to give his name.
"The Serb side defended itself as it always has and as it always will. Then the Moslems ran away as they always do."

U.S. sources on NATO duty in Bosnia told Reuters they believed both sides fired during the series of running skirmishes around Gajevi on Tuesday. The sources could not confirm Moslem reports that the Serbs used mortars, but said it was possible.
"It got out of hand. The Moslems were even firing at us at one point. They may have thought they were firing at the Serbs but they were shooting at us," Major Kershaw told Reuters.

Gajevi lies in an area known as the Zone Of Separation (ZOS), a band of former front-line territory stretching more than 1,000 kms (600-miles) across Bosnia. NATO has specific obligations to keep the peace in this tense zone under the terms of the Dayton peace accord.

Bosnia's formerly warring parties have agreed that refugees wanting to return to their homes inside the ZOS must submit applications to an international commission which would then ensure that those returning were actually from the area.
Refugees from Gajevi say they submitted applications more than three weeks ago which were not approved because the commission said they were incomplete, a charge Bosnian officials reject.
